name: SSB Interview
conductedBy: Services Selection Boards (Army, Navy, Air Force)
tagline: The 5-day officer selection process after NDA, CDS and AFCAT — understand every stage.

overview.about: The Services Selection Board (SSB) interview is a 5-day assessment of Officer Like Qualities for candidates who clear NDA, CDS, AFCAT and other officer entries. It includes screening (OIR + PPDT), psychology tests, group testing (GTO) tasks, a personal interview and a conference. Recommended candidates then undergo a medical examination.
eligibility: Candidates who clear the written exam (NDA, CDS, AFCAT) or are shortlisted under a direct entry (e.g. TES, NCC Special Entry, technical graduate entries)
Call letters are issued by the respective service — check joinindianarmy.nic.in, joinindiannavy.gov.in or the IAF portal
Bring all original documents listed in the call letter

pattern.note: OIR tests + PPDT (picture story, narration, group discussion). Not screened in → return home
TAT (12 pictures), WAT (60 words), SRT (60 situations), Self Description
GD, GPE, PGT, HGT, Snake Race, Lecturette, IO, Command Task, FGT
Held on one of the evenings of Days 2–4; based mainly on your PIQ
All assessors meet; results declared; recommended candidates go for medicals

overview.frequency: Batches run throughout the year after each written exam result

chapters.title: What the SSB is and how the 5 days run

cards.title: Why the SSB matters
cards.body: Clearing NDA, CDS or AFCAT only gets you an interview call. The **Services Selection Board (SSB)** decides whether you have the potential to become an officer. In NDA it carries 900 of 1800 marks; in CDS it carries 300 (IMA/INA/AFA) or 200 (OTA). It is the same process for Army, Navy and Air Force.

cards.title: The 5-day schedule
points: Reporting day: documents check, chest numbers, PIQ form
Day 1 — Screening: OIR test + PPDT. Those not screened in return home the same day
Day 2 — Psychology tests: TAT, WAT, SRT, Self Description
Days 3–4 — GTO tasks; personal interviews run on these evenings
Day 5 — Conference and results

cards.title: Three assessors, one picture
cards.body: You are assessed independently by three officers: the **Psychologist** (written psych tests), the **Group Testing Officer** (group and outdoor tasks) and the **Interviewing Officer** (personal interview). Each forms a view of the same qualities; consistency across all three is what gets you recommended.

cards.title: Where SSBs are held
cards.body: The Army runs Selection Centres at Prayagraj, Bhopal, Bengaluru and Kapurthala. The Air Force runs Air Force Selection Boards at Dehradun, Mysuru, Gandhinagar, Varanasi and Guwahati. The Navy has its own boards, including at Bengaluru, Bhopal, Coimbatore, Visakhapatnam and Kolkata. Your call letter names the centre.

cards.title: No 'right answers' — only you
cards.body: The SSB does not test knowledge; it looks for **Officer Like Qualities (OLQs)** that can be developed through training. Rehearsed, coaching-style answers usually show up as inconsistent. Being natural, honest and active is the best strategy.

cards.title: Tip
cards.body: Carry every document listed in your call letter (originals and copies), formal and sports clothes, and a watch. Missing documents can stop you before Day 1 even begins.

cards.q: On which day is the screening test (OIR + PPDT) held?
cards.explain: Screening happens on Day 1; only screened-in candidates stay for Days 2–5.

cards.q: Which three officers assess candidates at the SSB?
cards.explain: The three independent assessors are the Psychologist, the Group Testing Officer and the Interviewing Officer.

notes.p:
The **Services Selection Board (SSB)** is a five-day assessment that decides whether you have the potential to become an officer. The written exam (NDA, CDS, AFCAT or a direct entry) only earns you the call; the SSB carries heavy weight in the final merit — **900 of 1,800 marks in NDA**, and **300 marks (IMA/INA/AFA) or 200 (OTA) in CDS**.

The SSB is not a knowledge test. It looks for **Officer Like Qualities (OLQs)** — how you think, relate to people, act and persist. These qualities can be developed, which is why preparation starts months before the call letter arrives.

notes.h: The five days at a glance
notes.p: Every SSB follows the same broad schedule for Army, Navy and Air Force entries, though exact timings vary between boards. Knowing the flow in advance removes a lot of anxiety, because you know what is coming next and can rest and prepare accordingly.
points: Reporting day: document check, chest numbers, Personal Information Questionnaire (PIQ)
Day 1 — Screening: Officer Intelligence Rating (OIR) test and Picture Perception & Description Test (PPDT). Candidates not screened in return home the same day
Day 2 — Psychology: TAT, WAT, SRT and Self Description
Days 3–4 — Group Testing Officer (GTO) tasks; personal interviews usually run on these days
Day 5 — Conference and results; recommended candidates then stay for medicals

notes.p: You are assessed independently by three officers using three techniques:
points: Psychologist — through written tests (TAT, WAT, SRT, SD) that reveal your natural thinking
Group Testing Officer — through group discussions, planning and outdoor tasks that show how you behave in a team
Interviewing Officer — through a personal interview based mainly on your PIQ
At the conference, all three compare notes. Consistency across all three is what gets candidates recommended

notes.p:
Because three different techniques look at the same qualities, rehearsed or "coaching-style" responses tend to show up as **inconsistent** — a hero who is a fearless leader in TAT but a candidate who stays silent in the group discussion. Assessors are trained to spot this.

The winning approach is to **genuinely improve** before the SSB: get fit, read the news, speak in groups, take responsibility at home and college. Then, at the board, behave naturally. A calm, honest, active and cheerful candidate is exactly what the board wants to see.

Carry every document in your call letter (originals plus photocopies), passport photos, formal clothes for the interview and conference, sports kit (shoes, track suit, shorts), a watch, stationery and basic medicines. Missing documents can stop you before Day 1. Reach on time; the reporting day is part of the experience.

SSB centres are run by the Army (e.g. Prayagraj, Bhopal, Bengaluru, Kapurthala), the Air Force (Dehradun, Mysuru, Gandhinagar, Varanasi, Guwahati) and the Navy. Your call letter tells you where and when to report.
Keep this picture of the five days in mind as you prepare.
points: SSB = 900/1800 marks in NDA; 300 (or 200 for OTA) in CDS
Day 1 screening: OIR + PPDT
Day 2 psychology: TAT, WAT, SRT, SD
Days 3–4: GTO tasks and interviews
Day 5: conference and results
Three independent assessors; consistency matters
Genuine improvement beats rehearsed answers

cards.title: What OLQs are
cards.body: OLQs are the 15 qualities the SSB looks for. They are grouped into four factors. You don't need to 'act' them — they show up in how you think, mix with people, take action and keep going.

cards.title: Factor I — Planning & Organising
points: Effective Intelligence: practical problem-solving
Reasoning Ability: logical, quick grasp
Organising Ability: using resources systematically
Power of Expression: putting ideas across clearly

cards.title: Factor II — Social Adjustment
points: Social Adaptability: getting along with people and situations
Cooperation: working with the group towards a goal
Sense of Responsibility: dependable, owns duties

cards.title: Factor III — Social Effectiveness
points: Initiative: taking the first step
Self Confidence: belief in your ability, even under stress
Speed of Decision: deciding quickly and soundly
Ability to Influence the Group: others willingly follow you
Liveliness: cheerful, energetic, keeps morale up

cards.title: Factor IV — Dynamic
points: Determination: sticking to a goal despite obstacles
Courage: taking purposeful risks, physical and moral
Stamina: physical and mental endurance

cards.title: OLQs in daily life
cards.body: Organising your college fest shows Organising Ability and Initiative. Finishing a long run after a cramp shows Determination and Stamina. Admitting a mistake to your coach shows moral Courage and Sense of Responsibility. Build such real examples — they appear naturally in your interview and psych tests.

cards.title: Tip
cards.body: Pick 3–4 OLQs you are weakest in and work on them for months before the SSB (e.g. join a team sport for Cooperation, speak in class for Power of Expression). Real change shows; acting does not.

cards.q: How many Officer Like Qualities does the SSB assess?
cards.explain: There are 15 OLQs grouped into four factors.

cards.q: 'Speed of Decision' belongs to which factor?
cards.explain: Factor III (Social Effectiveness) has Initiative, Self Confidence, Speed of Decision, Ability to Influence the Group and Liveliness.

cards.q: Which of these is a 'Dynamic' factor quality?
cards.explain: Factor IV (Dynamic) is Determination, Courage and Stamina.

notes.p: **Officer Like Qualities** are 15 traits the SSB looks for, grouped into four factors. You don't need to "act" them; they show up naturally in how you plan, mix with people, take action and keep going. Every test — from PPDT to the conference — is designed to reveal them from a different angle.

The 15 OLQs are grouped into four factors. Learn them in this order — it follows a natural sequence: first you think and plan, then you fit in with people, then you influence and act, and finally you keep going when things get hard.
points: Factor I, Planning & Organising: Effective Intelligence, Reasoning Ability, Organising Ability, Power of Expression
Factor II, Social Adjustment: Social Adaptability, Cooperation, Sense of Responsibility
Factor III, Social Effectiveness: Initiative, Self Confidence, Speed of Decision, Ability to Influence the Group, Liveliness
Factor IV, Dynamic: Determination, Courage, Stamina

notes.h: What each factor looks like in practice
notes.p:
**Planning & Organising:** you solve practical problems with what is available, think logically, use time and resources well, and express your ideas clearly. In GPE, a sensible plan presented crisply shows this factor.

**Social Adjustment:** you get along with different people, work towards the group's goal rather than your own spotlight, and can be relied upon. In outdoor tasks, helping a teammate carry the load shows cooperation.

**Social Effectiveness:** you take the first step, stay confident under pressure, decide quickly, and people willingly follow you while you keep the mood positive. Giving the first workable idea in a group task — and then supporting a better one — shows initiative and influence.

**Dynamic:** you keep going despite obstacles, take purposeful physical and moral risks, and have physical and mental endurance. Attempting a difficult obstacle after failing once shows determination and courage.
OLQs grow with real experience, so build them deliberately over months:
points: Join a team sport — cooperation, liveliness, stamina
Volunteer to organise a college event — organising ability, responsibility, initiative
Speak in class and debates — power of expression, self-confidence
Run regularly and push your distance — determination, stamina
Admit mistakes openly and fix them — moral courage, responsibility
Keep a weekly diary of one example per factor; these become honest material for your interview

notes.p: OLQs are not about being loud. A candidate who shouts down others in a GD shows poor cooperation and social adaptability, even if they speak a lot. Nor are they about being perfect — the board looks for **trainable potential** and a balanced personality. Honest awareness of a weakness, with a real plan to improve it, is itself a sign of maturity.
Learn the 15 qualities in their four groups.
points: 15 OLQs in 4 factors
Planning & Organising: intelligence, reasoning, organising, expression
Social Adjustment: adaptability, cooperation, responsibility
Social Effectiveness: initiative, confidence, speed of decision, influence, liveliness
Dynamic: determination, courage, stamina
Develop them through real activities, not acting
Balance matters more than being loud

cards.title: What the PIQ is
cards.body: The **Personal Information Questionnaire** is filled in on reporting day or Day 1. It covers family, education with marks, sports, hobbies, NCC, positions of responsibility, previous SSB attempts and more. All three assessors see it, and the interviewer builds many questions from it.

cards.title: Be accurate and honest
cards.body: Every line in the PIQ can become an interview question. Write only what is true and what you can talk about in detail. If you write 'reading' as a hobby, expect to be asked about the last book you read and why you liked it.

cards.title: Fill it neatly
cards.body: Use capital letters where asked, avoid overwriting, and keep dates and marks consistent with your documents. A clean PIQ shows organising ability and attention to detail before you have said a word.

cards.title: Preparing PIQ answers
cards.body: Before the SSB, make a rough PIQ at home: list your marks year by year, sports achievements with dates, responsibilities held, and your family's details (education and occupation). Then practise talking about each item for one minute.

cards.title: Tip
cards.body: Keep a copy of your rough PIQ and revise it the night before the interview. Contradicting your own PIQ is one of the most common avoidable mistakes.

cards.q: Why is the PIQ form important?
options: Assessors, especially the interviewer, use it to frame questions
It is the OIR answer sheet
It is only for travel claims
cards.explain: The PIQ gives all assessors your background; the interviewing officer uses it heavily.

cards.q: If you list a hobby you don't really follow, the most likely result is:
options: Awkward, inconsistent answers in the interview
cards.explain: Detailed questions on that hobby will expose the gap and hurt your credibility.

notes.p: The **Personal Information Questionnaire (PIQ)** is a form filled in on reporting day or Day 1. It asks for family details (education and occupation of parents and siblings), your education with marks, sports and games, hobbies, NCC, positions of responsibility, previous SSB attempts and more. **All three assessors** see it, and the Interviewing Officer builds many questions from it — so it is the foundation of your interview.

Every line of your PIQ can become a question. If you write "reading" as a hobby, expect: "Which was the last book you read? Who wrote it? What did you learn from it?" If you write "football — college team", expect questions about your position, the team's results and the rules of the game.

Write only what is true and what you can discuss in detail for a few minutes. An exaggerated PIQ often unravels under follow-up questions and damages your credibility for the rest of the interview.
The PIQ is the first piece of your work the board sees, before you have said a word. Treat it like an official document, because it is one.
points: Use capital letters where asked and avoid overwriting or cutting
Keep dates, marks and percentages consistent with your documents
Read every instruction before writing — some fields have specific formats
If a field doesn't apply, follow the form's instruction (e.g. write 'NA' where asked) rather than leaving confusion
A neat, complete PIQ quietly shows organising ability and attention to detail

notes.h: Preparing a rough PIQ at home
notes.p: Before the SSB, make a **rough PIQ**:
points: Marks year by year from Class 10 onwards, with reasons for any dip
Sports and achievements with dates and levels (school, district, state)
Responsibilities held: class monitor, house captain, event organiser
Family: each member's education and occupation
Hobbies: what exactly you do, how often, and what you've gained
Your daily routine and your home town (history, problems, famous places)
Practise speaking for one minute on each item

notes.p:
Suppose your PIQ says: "Hobby — gardening." Likely questions: Which plants do you grow? What is the best season to sow them? How do you deal with pests? What did you learn from it? A good answer: "I grow tomatoes and chillies on our terrace. I start seedlings in February, use neem-oil spray against aphids, and I learned patience — plants don't grow on my schedule." Specific, true and reflective.

Common mistakes: listing five hobbies you rarely do; contradicting your PIQ in the interview; and copying the "ideal" answers of a friend.
Revise your rough PIQ the night before the interview.
points: All three assessors read your PIQ
Every line can become an interview question
Write only what you can discuss in depth
Keep dates and marks consistent with documents
Prepare a rough PIQ at home
Explain dips in marks honestly
Know your home town and family details well

cards.title: What OIR is
cards.body: The **Officer Intelligence Rating** test is usually two objective tests of verbal and non-verbal reasoning, taken against a tight clock on Day 1. Your OIR rating plus PPDT performance decides whether you are screened in.

cards.title: Common question types
points: Verbal: series, coding-decoding, analogies, odd one out, blood relations, directions
Non-verbal: figure series, mirror images, embedded figures, figure analogy, pattern completion

cards.title: Speed with accuracy
cards.body: Questions are easy individually; the challenge is time. Don't get stuck on one question — skip and return. Practising timed sets builds the rhythm you need.

cards.title: A quick series
cards.body: Find the next term: 3, 6, 11, 18, 27, ? The differences are 3, 5, 7, 9 — consecutive odd numbers. The next difference is 11, so the answer is **38**.

cards.title: Tip
cards.body: Practise 50 mixed reasoning questions a day for a month before your SSB. The same practice also helps the AFCAT reasoning section.

cards.q: Find the next term: 3, 6, 11, 18, 27, ?
cards.explain: Differences are 3, 5, 7, 9, so next is +11: 27 + 11 = 38.

cards.q: What does OIR stand for?
cards.explain: OIR = Officer Intelligence Rating, measured through verbal and non-verbal reasoning tests.

notes.p:
The **Officer Intelligence Rating (OIR)** test is usually given as two objective tests of **verbal and non-verbal reasoning**, taken on Day 1 against a tight clock. Your OIR rating, combined with your PPDT performance, decides whether you are **screened in**. The OIR rating also stays with you through the rest of the SSB as an indicator of your intelligence.

The questions are individually easy — the challenge is to answer many of them accurately in limited time.
Both tests mix question types, so practise all of them rather than only your favourites. The verbal test leans on language and number patterns; the non-verbal test on shapes and figures.
points: Verbal: number and letter series, coding–decoding, analogies, odd one out, blood relations, directions, ranking, simple arithmetic
Non-verbal: figure series, mirror and water images, embedded figures, figure analogies, pattern completion, odd figure out

notes.p:
**Example 1.** Find the next term: 3, 6, 11, 18, 27, ?
Step 1: Differences: 3, 5, 7, 9 — consecutive odd numbers.
Step 2: Next difference 11, so the answer is **38**.

**Example 2.** If MOTHER is coded as NPUIFS, how is SISTER coded?
Step 1: Each letter moves forward by one: M→N, O→P, T→U, H→I, E→F, R→S.
Step 2: S→T, I→J, S→T, T→U, E→F, R→S → **TJTUFS**.

**Example 3.** Odd one out: 121, 144, 169, 196, 210.
Step 1: 121 = 11², 144 = 12², 169 = 13², 196 = 14².
Step 2: 210 is not a perfect square → **210**.

Don't get stuck. If a question takes more than 30–40 seconds, skip it and return if time permits. Read instructions carefully — some questions ask for the "odd one out", others for the "similar one". In figure questions, track one change at a time (rotation, count, shading, position).

Build rhythm with daily practice: **50 mixed questions a day** for at least a month, timed. The same practice helps the AFCAT reasoning section. Keep a list of question types where you are slow and drill them.

Day 1 can be tense — many candidates are screened out on the same day. Sleep well the night before and eat a light breakfast. Treat the OIR like a practice set you've done a hundred times. If you hit a hard question early, remember that everyone faces the same paper; staying calm and moving on is part of the test.
Speed comes from daily timed practice.
points: OIR + PPDT = screening on Day 1
Verbal and non-verbal reasoning, tight time limit
Series: check differences first
Coding: find the shift for each letter
Skip after 30–40 seconds; come back later
50 timed questions a day for a month
Sleep well; stay calm

cards.title: How PPDT works
cards.body: **Picture Perception & Description Test**: a hazy picture is shown for 30 seconds. You get 1 minute to note the characters you perceive (number, age, gender, mood) and 3 minutes to write a story. Then the group sits together for individual narrations and a group discussion.

cards.title: Writing a good story
cards.body: Base the story on what is seen in the picture. Answer: what led to the situation, what is happening now, and how it ends. Give the main character a positive, practical role — someone who solves a problem using available resources.

cards.title: Narration
cards.body: Each candidate narrates their story in about a minute. Speak clearly, keep eye contact with the group, and finish within time. Confidence and clarity matter more than a dramatic plot.

cards.title: Group discussion
cards.body: The group tries to agree on a common story. Contribute early, listen, build on good ideas and help the group reach a conclusion. Shouting over others or staying silent both hurt you.

cards.title: Sample PPDT outline
cards.body: Picture: a few people near a damaged bridge. Story: Rahul, 22, a civil engineering student, notices villagers stranded after floods. He organises volunteers, arranges a temporary crossing with ropes and boats, and informs the district authorities. By evening everyone is safe and repair work begins.

cards.title: Tip
cards.body: Practise with random pictures from newspapers: 30 seconds look, 1 minute characters, 3 minutes story. Then narrate it aloud in under a minute. Ten days of this transforms your screening performance.

cards.q: For how long is the PPDT picture shown?
cards.explain: The picture is shown for 30 seconds.

cards.q: In PPDT group discussion, the best approach is to:
options: Dominate and never let others speak
Contribute, listen and help the group reach a common story
cards.explain: Assessors look for balanced participation that moves the group forward.

notes.p:
In the **Picture Perception & Description Test**, a hazy picture is shown for **30 seconds**. You then get **1 minute** to note the characters you perceive (number, approximate age, gender and mood) in a box, and **3 minutes** to write a story. Later the group sits in a circle; each candidate **narrates** their story (about a minute), and then the group holds a **discussion** to agree on a common story.

PPDT and OIR together decide screening, so PPDT is your first chance to show OLQs to the assessors.
Your story should be **based on what is seen in the picture** — don't ignore the main figures. Answer three questions:
points: What led to the situation? (past)
What is happening now? (present)
What is the outcome? (future)
Give the main character (hero) a positive, practical role, close to your own age
Use available resources; avoid miracles, magic or lucky coincidences
Keep it simple and realistic; one clear theme is better than five plot twists

notes.p:
**Picture:** a few people near a damaged bridge after rain.

**Characters noted:** 4 persons — 1 male (~22, positive), others villagers (mixed ages, worried).

**Story:** Rahul, 22, a civil engineering student, was visiting his village when heavy rains damaged the only bridge to the market. He found villagers stranded on the far bank. He gathered four volunteers, collected ropes and two fishing boats, and set up a guided crossing — elderly and children first. He informed the district administration by phone and asked for engineers. By evening, everyone had crossed safely, and the next week repair work started with Rahul helping the engineers survey the site.

Notice: a clear past, present and future; practical actions; cooperation; and a realistic outcome.

**Narration:** speak clearly at a steady pace, keep eye contact with the group, and finish within the time. Confidence and clarity matter more than a dramatic plot.

**Group discussion:** the aim is to reach a **common story**. Enter early with a sensible point, listen to others, build on good ideas ("Adding to what number 5 said…"), and help the group conclude. Shouting over others, repeating your own story stubbornly, or staying silent all hurt you. If the discussion becomes chaotic, calmly suggesting a structure ("Let's first agree on what the picture shows") is a strong move.

Use random pictures from newspapers or magazines: look for 30 seconds, note characters in 1 minute, write a story in 3 minutes, then narrate it aloud in under a minute. Practise group discussions with 4–6 friends weekly. Ten days of consistent practice noticeably improves screening performance.
Practise the timing until it feels natural.
points: 30 s picture, 1 min characters, 3 min story
Past → present → future
Positive, practical hero close to your age
Use available resources; no miracles
Narrate clearly in about a minute
In discussion: contribute early, listen, help conclude
Practise with newspaper pictures daily

cards.title: TAT format
cards.body: You are shown **12 pictures** — usually 11 pictures and 1 blank slide. Each is shown for 30 seconds and you get **4 minutes** to write a story. For the blank slide you write a story of your own choice.

cards.title: What the psychologist reads
cards.body: Your stories reveal how you think, feel and act. The psychologist looks for themes repeated across stories — is your hero practical, socially aware, active and resilient? Consistency over 12 stories reveals your natural OLQs.

cards.title: Structure of a story
cards.body: Past (what led to it), present (what the hero is doing), future (outcome). Keep the hero close to your age and background. Show realistic actions with available resources, not superhero feats or lucky coincidences.

cards.title: Weak vs better
cards.body: Weak: 'He saw the accident and felt sad.' Better: 'Arjun saw the accident, called 112, gave first aid to the injured rider, guided traffic until the ambulance arrived, and later helped police note witness details.' Action, responsibility and a clear outcome.

cards.title: Tip
cards.body: Practise writing 2–3 stories a day with a timer. Read your stories after a week — if every hero is the same superhuman, make them more realistic.

cards.q: How many pictures are typically shown in TAT, including the blank slide?
cards.explain: Usually 11 pictures plus 1 blank slide, for a total of 12.

cards.q: How long do you get to write each TAT story?
cards.explain: Each picture is shown for 30 seconds, followed by 4 minutes of writing.

notes.p:
In the **Thematic Apperception Test**, you are shown **12 pictures** — usually 11 pictures and 1 blank slide. Each is shown for **30 seconds**, and you get **4 minutes** to write a story. For the blank slide, you write a story of your own choice — many candidates write about something from their own life or aspirations.

The pictures are deliberately ambiguous, so what you "see" and write reveals how you think, feel and act.

The psychologist looks for **themes repeated across all 12 stories**. Is your hero practical? Socially aware? Active rather than passive? Resilient after setbacks? Twelve stories written under time pressure reveal your natural patterns — one good story cannot hide eleven passive ones, and an obviously "manufactured" superhero in every story looks unrealistic.
With only four minutes per picture, a fixed structure saves time and keeps every story complete. Practise this frame until you use it without thinking.
points: Past: what led to this situation (one or two lines)
Present: what the hero is thinking and doing — the main part
Future: a realistic outcome and what the hero learned or achieved
Hero: close to your age, gender and background; give a name and age
Actions: practical, step by step, using available resources and other people
Outcome: positive but believable — not 'he became the Prime Minister'

notes.h: Weak vs better: a worked example
notes.p:
**Picture:** a young man standing near a crowd on a road.

**Weak:** "He saw the accident and felt sad. He thought the government should do something. He went home." — passive, no action, no outcome.

**Better:** "Arjun, 21, was returning from college when he saw a motorcyclist lying injured after a collision. He called 112, asked the crowd to step back, and gave first aid to stop the bleeding. He guided traffic with two bystanders until the ambulance arrived, then informed the rider's family using the phone found in his pocket. Later, he helped the police note witness details. The rider recovered, and Arjun's college invited a doctor to train students in first aid." — action, responsibility, cooperation and a constructive outcome.

Practise **2–3 stories a day** with a timer (30 seconds viewing, 4 minutes writing). After a week, reread them. If every hero is identical and superhuman, make them more realistic; if many end without resolution, add outcomes.

Traps: copying memorised stories (they rarely fit the picture), writing negative endings repeatedly, making the hero passive, and running out of time — always leave a line for the outcome.
Write at least 40 practice stories before your SSB.
points: 12 pictures (11 + 1 blank); 30 s view, 4 min write
Psychologist reads themes across all stories
Past → present → future
Hero near your age; practical actions
Realistic, positive outcomes
Avoid memorised and superhero stories
Always finish with an outcome

cards.title: Word Association Test (WAT)
cards.body: 60 words are shown one after another, **15 seconds each**. You write the first meaningful sentence that comes to mind. Speed forces your genuine thinking to show, so practise to make positive, practical thinking your natural habit.

cards.title: Good WAT responses
cards.body: Keep sentences short, positive and realistic. Avoid preaching ('One should always…'), avoid copying the same sentence pattern, and don't leave too many blanks. A sentence can be an observation, an action or a value.

cards.title: Situation Reaction Test (SRT)
cards.body: **60 everyday situations in 30 minutes**. For each, write what you would do in a few words. The psychologist looks for practical, quick, responsible and socially sensible reactions.

cards.title: SRT sample
cards.body: Situation: 'On his way to an exam, he sees an injured person on the road. He…' Response: 'called an ambulance, gave first aid, informed a nearby police officer, then reached the exam centre and explained the delay.' It handles both duties practically.

cards.title: WAT samples
cards.body: 'Fear' → 'Preparation reduces fear before a task.' 'Army' → 'The Army helps citizens during floods.' 'Fail' → 'He analysed his failure and improved.' Simple, positive, realistic.

cards.title: Tip
cards.body: Practise WAT with a 15-second timer and SRT in sets of 60 in 30 minutes. Attempting most situations matters — leaving many blank suggests slow decision-making.

cards.q: How many words are shown in WAT and for how long each?
cards.explain: WAT has 60 words, each shown for 15 seconds.

cards.q: How many situations are given in SRT and in how much time?
cards.explain: SRT has 60 situations to be answered in 30 minutes.

notes.p: In the **WAT**, **60 words** are shown one after another, **15 seconds each**. You write the first meaningful sentence that comes to mind. Because there is no time to manufacture answers, your genuine thinking shows. The goal of preparation is to make **positive, practical thinking your natural habit**, not to memorise sentences.
Fifteen seconds is enough for one short sentence. What matters is that the sentence reflects a healthy, active outlook — and that it reads like you, not like a book of quotations.
points: Short, clear and complete: a subject and a verb
Positive or constructive, but realistic — not preachy
Varied: observation, action or value, not the same pattern every time
Avoid 'One should always…' and 'We must…' sermons
Avoid copying the word into a dictionary definition

Examples: 'Fear' → 'Preparation reduces fear before a task.' 'Army' → 'The Army helps citizens during floods.' 'Fail' → 'He analysed his failure and improved.' 'Night' → 'Sentries stay alert through the night.'

notes.p:
The **SRT** gives **60 everyday situations in 30 minutes** — about 30 seconds each. For each, write what you would do, briefly. The psychologist looks for **practical, quick, responsible and socially sensible** reactions. Attempting most situations matters: leaving many blank suggests slow decision-making.

**Example 1.** "On his way to an exam, he sees an injured person on the road. He…"
Response: "called an ambulance, gave first aid, informed a nearby policeman, then reached the exam centre and explained the delay."
It handles both duties practically.

**Example 2.** "He is the captain of his team and two players start fighting before the final. He…"
Response: "separated them calmly, heard both sides, settled the issue, reminded them of the team goal and played the final together."

Use telegraphic language — short phrases, no full essays. A good reaction usually: (1) handles the immediate problem, (2) involves the right people or authorities where needed, and (3) completes the original task if possible. Avoid unrealistic heroics ("fought ten dacoits alone") and avoid escaping responsibility ("ignored it and left").

Practise WAT with a **15-second timer** — have a friend show words, or use a slideshow. Practise SRT in sets of **60 in 30 minutes**. Alternate days between the two in the last month. After each set, review: are your responses varied, practical and consistent with the way you actually behave?

Traps: memorised sentences that don't fit the word; many blanks; negative responses on emotionally loaded words ("death", "failure"); and answers that contradict your TAT heroes and interview.
Practise with a timer — speed is the whole test.
points: WAT: 60 words × 15 seconds
First meaningful, positive, realistic sentence
No sermons; vary your sentence patterns
SRT: 60 situations in 30 minutes
Handle the problem, involve the right people, complete the task
Attempt most situations
Stay consistent with your TAT and interview

cards.title: SD format
cards.body: In about **15 minutes** you write five short paragraphs: what your **parents** think of you, what your **teachers or employer** think, what your **friends** think, what **you** think of yourself, and what **qualities you want to develop**.

cards.title: Be honest and balanced
cards.body: Mention real strengths and a few genuine weaknesses with what you are doing about them. An SD with only praise looks unrealistic. The psychologist compares your SD with your TAT, WAT and SRT for consistency.

cards.title: Sample line
cards.body: Friends: 'My friends see me as dependable and someone who plans group trips well. They also say I can be impatient when things get delayed, which I am working on by planning extra buffer time.'

cards.title: Tip
cards.body: Ask your parents, a teacher and two friends what they actually think of you before the SSB. Their real views make your SD honest and give you material for the interview too.

cards.q: How many parts does the Self Description test have?
cards.explain: Parents, teachers/employer, friends, self, and qualities you wish to develop — five parts.

cards.q: A good Self Description should be:
options: Honest, with strengths and genuine areas to improve
cards.explain: Balanced, honest descriptions are consistent with your other tests and look credible.

notes.p: In the **Self Description Test**, you get about **15 minutes** to write five short paragraphs:
points: What your parents think of you
What your teachers or employer think of you
What your friends think of you
What you think of yourself
What qualities you want to develop

notes.p:
Mention **real strengths and a few genuine weaknesses**, along with what you are doing about them. A description full of praise looks unrealistic and suggests poor self-awareness. The psychologist compares your SD with your TAT, WAT and SRT — and the interviewer may ask about it too — so consistency matters.

Each paragraph should be specific. Instead of "My parents think I am good," write what they actually say and why.

**Parents:** "My parents see me as responsible because I manage my younger sister's studies and handle bank work for the family. They feel I spend too much time on my phone, and I now keep it away after 9 pm."

**Teachers:** "My physics teacher considers me hard-working and good at practical work. She has told me to ask doubts in class instead of waiting till the end."

**Friends:** "My friends see me as dependable and someone who plans group trips well. They also say I can be impatient when things get delayed, which I am working on by keeping buffer time."

**Self:** "I am disciplined about fitness and enjoy leading small teams. I need to become more patient and to speak more confidently in large groups."

**Qualities to develop:** "Public speaking, patience and better time management in exams."

Before the SSB, **ask** your parents, a teacher and two friends what they genuinely think of you — strengths and weaknesses. Their real views make your SD honest and give you material for the interview. Write a draft, keep each paragraph to 4–6 lines, and practise finishing all five within 15 minutes.

Traps: leaving paragraphs incomplete; listing only adjectives without examples; claiming weaknesses that are disguised strengths ("I work too hard"); and contradicting your PIQ.

Weaknesses are not a trap — how you present them shows self-awareness. Use a simple pattern: **name the weakness honestly, give a small example, and state what you are doing about it.**

Good: "I tend to leave assignments for the last two days. Since last semester I have been breaking them into daily targets, and I submitted my last project three days early."

Avoid: fake weaknesses ("I am too honest"), serious issues written carelessly without any action, and long lists of faults. Two or three genuine, ordinary weaknesses — impatience, hesitation in large groups, untidy handwriting, poor time management — with real steps taken are enough.
Finish all five parts — an incomplete SD looks disorganised.
points: Five parts in about 15 minutes
Parents, teachers, friends, self, qualities to develop
Real strengths + genuine weaknesses + action taken
Specific examples, not just adjectives
Ask people what they think before the SSB
Stay consistent with PIQ and psych tests

cards.title: Group Discussion
cards.body: Usually two rounds on social or current topics. Speak early with a clear point, back it with facts or examples, invite quieter members and help the group reach a conclusion. Quality and relevance beat volume.

cards.title: Group Planning Exercise (GPE)
cards.body: Also called the Military Planning Exercise. The GTO explains a model showing an area with several problems (e.g. an accident, a bomb threat, a fire) and limited resources. You first write your own plan, then the group discusses and one candidate presents the group plan.

cards.title: How to plan in GPE
points: Prioritise problems: life first, then property, then other tasks
Use resources and timings realistically (speed, distance)
Give a clear sequence and who does what
Keep the overall aim in mind while handling emergencies

cards.title: Lecturette
cards.body: Pick one topic from a card with **four topics**, prepare for **3 minutes**, then speak for **3 minutes** to the group. Structure: introduction, 2–3 main points, conclusion. Choose a topic you can genuinely talk about, not the hardest one.

cards.title: Tip
cards.body: Read the newspaper daily and form opinions on major issues. Practise lecturettes in front of a mirror or friends with a timer — 3 minutes passes quickly.

cards.q: In GPE, what should usually get top priority?
cards.explain: Human life comes first, then property and other tasks.

cards.q: In the lecturette, how long do you speak?
cards.explain: You get 3 minutes to prepare and 3 minutes to speak.

notes.p: GTO tasks usually begin with **group discussions**, often two rounds on social or current topics. The GTO watches how you contribute, listen and help the group function — not who speaks the most.
points: Speak early with a clear, relevant point
Support your point with a fact or example
Listen and build on others' ideas; disagree politely with reasons
Invite quieter members in when the discussion stalls
Help the group summarise or reach a conclusion near the end
Avoid shouting, interrupting repeatedly or going off-topic

notes.p: The **Group Planning Exercise** (also called the Military Planning Exercise) uses a model of an area — villages, roads, a river, a railway line — with several problems happening at once (e.g. an accident, a fire, a bomb threat) and limited resources and time. Steps: the GTO explains the model and narrative; you read the situation; you **write your own plan**; then the group discusses and agrees on a common plan; finally one candidate (sometimes chosen by the GTO) presents it.
A GPE plan is judged on whether it is sensible, workable and clearly explained. Use this checklist while writing your individual plan and again during the group discussion.
points: Prioritise problems: human life first, then vital property and infrastructure, then other tasks
Check the time available and calculate travel times realistically (time = distance ÷ speed)
Allocate resources and people clearly — who does what, by which route
Keep the overall aim in mind while handling emergencies
Example: a vehicle travelling 18 km at 36 km/h takes 18 ÷ 36 = 0.5 hours = 30 minutes — check that it arrives before the deadline
In discussion, support a better plan if one emerges — stubbornness costs more than flexibility

notes.p:
In the **lecturette**, you pick one topic from a card with **four topics**, prepare for **3 minutes**, and speak for **3 minutes** to the group. Choose a topic you can genuinely talk about rather than the "hardest" one.

Simple structure: **Introduction** (what the topic is and why it matters — 30 seconds), **two or three main points** with examples (2 minutes), and **conclusion** (your view or the way forward — 30 seconds). Stand straight, make eye contact around the group, and speak at a steady pace. Finishing on time with a clear conclusion is better than rushing through ten points.

Read a newspaper daily and form a view on 3 major issues each week. Prepare short notes on common lecturette themes: defence, environment, technology, sports, education, India's neighbours, and social issues. Practise lecturettes in front of a mirror or friends with a timer — 3 minutes passes quickly. For GPE, practise speed–distance–time calculations until they are automatic.
Quality and relevance beat volume in every indoor task.
points: GD: speak early, support with facts, listen, help conclude
GPE: write your own plan, then agree on a group plan
Priority: life → property → other tasks
Calculate travel times realistically
Lecturette: 4 topics, 3 min prep, 3 min speaking
Intro → 2–3 points → conclusion
Read the newspaper daily

cards.title: Progressive Group Task (PGT)
cards.body: The group crosses a series of obstacles of increasing difficulty using helping materials (plank, rope, ballie, load). Rules apply: coloured parts are out of bounds, and the load must be carried across. The GTO watches ideas, teamwork and acceptance by the group.

cards.title: Half Group Task (HGT)
cards.body: Like PGT but with the group split into two halves, so each candidate has more chance to contribute. Give your idea clearly, show it physically if needed, and work actively on others' good ideas too.

cards.title: Group Obstacle Race (Snake Race)
cards.body: Groups race over obstacles while carrying a heavy snake-like rope, with rules on how it is held. It tests group spirit, liveliness, stamina and cooperation. Cheer your team, take your share of the load and help others cross.

cards.title: Individual Obstacles (IO)
cards.body: **10 numbered obstacles in 3 minutes**, each worth points equal to its number. Plan your order beforehand, tackle obstacles you are confident in and keep moving. Attempting many with energy shows courage and stamina.

cards.title: Command Task and Final Group Task
cards.body: In the Command Task you are the commander: you choose a couple of subordinates from your group and lead them over an obstacle. The Final Group Task (FGT) is a last group obstacle where the GTO gives everyone one more chance to show their qualities.

cards.title: Tip
cards.body: Physical fitness matters: run 3–5 km regularly, do pull-ups, push-ups and jumps for at least 2 months before the SSB. Learn to tie a few simple knots and how to use the helping materials.

cards.q: How many obstacles are attempted in Individual Obstacles, and in how much time?
cards.explain: IO has 10 numbered obstacles to be attempted in 3 minutes.

cards.q: In the Command Task, the candidate:
options: Leads chosen subordinates over an obstacle
cards.explain: You act as commander and lead the subordinates you select.

cards.q: The Snake Race mainly tests:
cards.explain: Carrying the 'snake' over obstacles as a team reveals cooperation, liveliness and stamina.

notes.p:
In the **PGT**, the group crosses a series of obstacles of **increasing difficulty** using helping materials such as a plank, a rope, a ballie (wooden pole) and a load. Rules apply — for example, coloured parts of structures are out of bounds, and the load must be carried across. The GTO watches your ideas, physical involvement, cooperation and how readily the group accepts your suggestions.

Good behaviour: give your idea clearly and briefly; if the group doesn't take it, work wholeheartedly on the plan they choose; follow the rules and remind others politely; keep energy up.

notes.h: Half Group Task and Snake Race
notes.p:
The **Half Group Task (HGT)** is like the PGT but with the group split into two halves, so each candidate has more chance to contribute. Show your idea physically if needed, and stay active throughout.

The **Group Obstacle Race (Snake Race)** has groups racing over obstacles while carrying a heavy, snake-like rope bundle, with rules on how it is held. It tests group spirit, liveliness, stamina and cooperation. Cheer your team, take your share of the load, help others over obstacles and keep moving.

In **Individual Obstacles**, you attempt **10 numbered obstacles in 3 minutes**; each is worth points equal to its number. Typical obstacles include ramps, jumps, rope climbs, a "Tarzan swing", a "Burma bridge" and a commando walk (the exact set varies by board).

Tips: plan your order beforehand, starting near higher-value obstacles you are confident in; keep moving rather than standing at one obstacle; and if you fail, try again or move to the next one. Attempting many with energy shows courage and stamina.

notes.h: Command Task and Final Group Task
notes.p:
In the **Command Task**, you are the commander. You choose one or two subordinates from your group and lead them across an obstacle using helping materials. The GTO may give you hints or constraints. Brief your subordinates clearly, involve their ideas, stay calm if the first attempt fails, and keep control without shouting.

The **Final Group Task (FGT)** is a last group obstacle where the GTO gives everyone one more chance to show their qualities. Treat it as seriously as the first task.

Outdoor tasks demand real fitness: tired candidates stop contributing ideas as well as effort. Start training at least two months before your SSB, and know the common mistakes that cost candidates in the GTO's eyes.
points: Run 3–5 km regularly for at least two months before the SSB
Build upper-body strength: pull-ups, push-ups, rope climbing if available
Practise jumps and balance (walking on a narrow beam)
Learn a few simple knots and how planks and ropes are used on structures
Trap: pushing your idea even after the group rejects it
Trap: breaking rules (touching coloured areas) to save time
Trap: standing idle while others work — stay physically involved

notes.p: Fitness and team spirit carry you through outdoor tasks.
points: PGT: obstacles of increasing difficulty with helping materials
HGT: half group, more chance to contribute
Snake race: group spirit, stamina, cooperation
IO: 10 obstacles in 3 minutes, points = obstacle number
Command Task: you lead chosen subordinates
FGT: one last group chance
Follow the rules; support the group's plan

cards.title: Format
cards.body: The interview is conducted by the Interviewing Officer — often the President or Deputy President of the board — usually on Day 2, 3 or 4 evenings. It can last from about 30 minutes to over an hour and is based mainly on your PIQ.

cards.title: Rapid-fire questions
cards.body: The interviewer may ask 8–10 questions in one breath about school, friends, family, achievements and failures. Note them mentally in order, answer each briefly and honestly. Missing one or two is fine; making things up is not.

cards.title: Areas to prepare
points: Yourself: strengths, weaknesses, daily routine
Education: marks, favourite/least favourite subjects and why
Family: members' education and occupations
Hobbies, sports, NCC, responsibilities
Why the Armed Forces / your chosen service
Current affairs and your home town/state

cards.title: Body language
cards.body: Sit straight, maintain natural eye contact, speak at a steady pace and smile when appropriate. Say 'I don't know, sir' rather than guessing. Being calm and honest under pressure is itself an OLQ.

cards.title: Answering 'Why the Army?'
cards.body: Avoid clichés like 'to serve the nation' alone. Better: 'My uncle is a JCO and I have seen how disciplined and purposeful his life is. NCC camps showed me I enjoy leading teams outdoors, and I want a career where that is my everyday job.' Personal, specific, true.

cards.title: Tip
cards.body: Do mock interviews with friends or family using your rough PIQ. Ask them to fire 8 questions at once and practise answering in order.

cards.q: The SSB personal interview is mainly based on:
cards.explain: The interviewing officer uses your PIQ to frame most questions.

cards.q: If you don't know an answer in the interview, you should:
cards.explain: Honesty is valued; bluffing damages credibility.

notes.p: The **personal interview** is conducted by the Interviewing Officer — often the President or Deputy President of the board. It typically takes place on the evenings of Days 2, 3 or 4 (some boards schedule interviews at other times). It can last from about 30 minutes to over an hour and is based mainly on your **PIQ**. The aim is to understand you as a person: your background, how you think, and how you handle pressure.

The interviewer may ask **8–10 questions in one breath** — about school, friends, family, achievements and failures. Note them mentally in order (some candidates use a finger-count), then answer each **briefly and honestly** in the same order. Missing one or two is fine; making things up is not.

**Example:** "Tell me about your school, your best friend, your favourite teacher and why, your marks in Class 10 and 12, the games you played, and one thing you regret." Answer each in 2–3 lines, in order, then pause for follow-ups.
Most questions fall into a few predictable areas. Prepare each with honest, specific answers and real examples, so you can speak naturally rather than reciting.
points: Yourself: strengths, weaknesses, daily routine
Education: marks, favourite and least favourite subjects and why
Family: members' education and occupations
Hobbies, sports, NCC, responsibilities held
Why the Armed Forces and why your chosen service
Current affairs, defence news, and your home town and state
Previous SSB attempts (if any): what you learned and improved

notes.p:
Avoid one-line clichés like "to serve the nation" on their own. A strong answer is **personal, specific and true**.

**Example:** "My uncle is a JCO, and I have seen how disciplined and purposeful his life is. NCC camps showed me that I enjoy leading teams outdoors, and I want a career where that is my everyday job. I also like the challenge and variety of postings across the country."

Sit straight, maintain natural eye contact, speak at a steady pace and smile when appropriate. Say "I don't know, sir" instead of guessing — being calm and honest under pressure is itself an OLQ. If you made a mistake earlier in the SSB, own it.

Traps: contradicting your PIQ; memorised speeches; arguing with the interviewer; and pretending to know current affairs you haven't read.
Use these for mock interviews with family or friends. Answer each in under a minute, then let them ask a follow-up based on your answer:
points: Tell me about yourself and your family
What did you do yesterday from morning to night?
Which subject did you find hardest, and how did you handle it?
Tell me about a time you failed. What did you learn?
Who is your role model, and why?
What are the main problems of your home town, and how would you solve one?
If you are not recommended, what will you do?

notes.p: Practise with mock interviews before the SSB.
points: Based mainly on your PIQ
Rapid-fire: remember the order, answer briefly
Prepare self, education, family, hobbies, service choice
'Why the Forces?' — personal and specific
Say 'I don't know' rather than guessing
Natural eye contact, steady pace
Never contradict your PIQ

cards.title: The conference (Day 5)
cards.body: All assessors sit together. Each candidate is called in, usually in formal dress, and asked a few simple questions such as 'How was your stay?' or 'Anything you'd like to say?'. The board then discusses each case and decides who is recommended.

cards.title: How to handle it
cards.body: Be calm, cheerful and brief. Don't argue or plead. If asked about a weak task, admit it honestly and say what you learned. The decision is mostly made from your performance across the five days.

cards.title: Results and medicals
cards.body: Results are announced on the same day. Recommended candidates stay for a medical examination by a Special Medical Board, which takes a few more days. If declared unfit, you can usually apply for an Appeal or Review Medical Board as per the rules.

cards.title: After recommendation
cards.body: Being recommended and medically fit puts you on the **merit list** — for NDA and CDS, combined with your written score. Joining depends on your merit rank and the number of vacancies. Keep checking the official website for joining instructions.

cards.title: Tip
cards.body: Not recommended? Many successful officers cleared the SSB on their second or later attempt. Note what you felt went wrong, work on it for months, and reapply.

cards.q: When are SSB results usually announced?
cards.explain: Results are declared on conference day (Day 5).

cards.q: A candidate declared medically unfit by the Special Medical Board can usually:
options: Apply for an Appeal/Review Medical Board as per rules
Retake the SSB the next day
cards.explain: Rules provide for an appeal or review medical board within a set time.

notes.p:
On the final day, all assessors sit together for the **conference**. Each candidate is called in, usually in formal dress, and asked a few simple questions such as "How was your stay?", "Did you face any problems?" or "Anything you'd like to say?". The board then discusses each candidate and decides who is **recommended**.

The decision is made mostly from your performance across all five days. The conference is a final, brief look at you — not a second interview.
The conference usually lasts only a few minutes per candidate. A short, sincere and composed presence is all you need.
points: Be calm, cheerful and brief
Answer honestly; don't argue or plead
If asked about a weak task, admit it and say what you learned
If asked whether you'd like to try again or join another entry, answer sincerely
Thank the board when leaving; walk out confidently

notes.p:
Results are usually announced the **same day**. Recommended candidates stay for a **medical examination by a Special Medical Board (SMB)**, which takes a few more days. If declared unfit, you can usually apply for an **Appeal Medical Board** and, in some cases, a **Review Medical Board**, as per the rules in force.

Medical tips: check your eyesight, hearing, weight-for-height and dental health months before the SSB, and treat fixable issues (like wax in the ears or minor dental problems) early. Exact medical standards differ by service and entry, so read the notification and official medical guidelines.

Being recommended and medically fit places you on the **merit list** — for NDA and CDS, combined with your written score. Final joining depends on your merit rank and the number of vacancies, which vary every course. Keep checking the official websites for the merit list and joining instructions, and keep your documents ready.

Many successful officers cleared the SSB on their second or later attempt. Within a day, write down what you felt went wrong in each test while it is fresh. Then work on those areas for months — fitness, communication, reading, real responsibilities — and reapply. Improvement shows; repeating the same approach usually produces the same result.

Wear clean formal clothes — a well-ironed shirt and trousers (or equivalent formal attire), polished shoes and neat grooming. Enter when called, greet the board, sit only when asked, and keep your hands still and posture straight. Speak clearly, even if your voice feels nervous.

Most importantly, keep perspective. By Day 5 your performance is largely recorded. Use the conference to show the same calm, cheerful person the board has observed all week — and whatever the result, thank the staff before you leave. That courtesy reflects the officer you want to become.
The conference is short — your five days decide the result.
points: All assessors decide together at the conference
Be calm, brief and honest
Results usually the same day
Recommended candidates undergo SMB medicals
Appeal (and possibly Review) Medical Board if declared unfit
Merit list combines written score and SSB (NDA/CDS)
Not recommended? Analyse, improve, reapply

chapters.title: How to prepare: a day-by-day plan

cards.title: Start early — OLQs take time
cards.body: Begin SSB preparation alongside your written exam, not after the result. Physical fitness, communication and current affairs take months to build, and these are exactly what the SSB rewards.

cards.title: Weeks 1–4: foundation
points: Daily: 3–5 km run, push-ups, pull-ups
Read a newspaper and note 3 issues with your opinion
Practise 50 OIR questions
Write your rough PIQ and talk about each line

cards.title: Weeks 5–8: test practice
points: Daily: 2 TAT stories, 1 PPDT, 60 WAT words or 60 SRTs (alternate days)
Two GD or lecturette practices a week with friends
Self Description draft after asking parents, teachers, friends
Mock interviews once a week

cards.title: At the SSB, day by day
points: Reporting: documents ready, fill PIQ carefully
Day 1: stay calm in OIR; write a clear, positive PPDT story
Day 2: attempt as many WAT/SRT items as you can; be yourself
Days 3–4: be active and cooperative in GTO; rest well before the interview
Day 5: stay relaxed in the conference

cards.title: Life at the centre
cards.body: Mix with your group, help others, eat and sleep well. The board observes you informally too. Avoid discussing 'tricks' with other candidates the night before tests — it only adds confusion.

cards.title: Tip
cards.body: Record yourself speaking for 2 minutes on a topic once a week. Watching it back is the quickest way to improve clarity, pace and body language.

cards.q: When should you ideally start SSB preparation?
cards.explain: Fitness and communication take months to build, so start alongside the written exam.

cards.q: Which daily habit most helps GD, lecturette and the interview together?
options: Reading the newspaper and forming opinions
cards.explain: Current affairs with your own opinions feeds GD, lecturette and interview answers.

notes.p: Begin SSB preparation **alongside your written exam**, not after the result. Physical fitness, communication skills and awareness of current affairs take months to build, and these are exactly what the SSB rewards. A two-month plan before the SSB, on top of daily habits built earlier, works well for most candidates.
The first month builds the base that every test depends on: fitness, awareness, reasoning speed and a clear picture of yourself through the PIQ.
points: Daily: 3–5 km run, push-ups, pull-ups and stretching
Read a newspaper; note 3 issues each week with your own opinion
Practise 50 OIR questions a day, timed
Write your rough PIQ and practise talking about each line for a minute
Speak for 2 minutes daily on any topic — record and review once a week

notes.p: In the second month, shift to timed practice of the actual tests while keeping the foundation habits going. Review your work weekly to spot patterns you want to change.
points: Daily: 2 TAT stories and 1 PPDT story with a timer
Alternate days: 60 WAT words or 60 SRTs in 30 minutes
Two GD or lecturette practices a week with friends
Draft your Self Description after asking parents, teachers and friends
One mock interview a week using your rough PIQ, including rapid-fire questions
Continue fitness: add jumps, rope work and balance practice

notes.h: At the SSB, day by day
notes.p: At the board, your preparation is done; the aim now is to stay rested, calm and natural so your real qualities show.
points: Reporting: documents ready; fill the PIQ carefully and neatly
Day 1: stay calm in OIR; write a clear, positive PPDT story and contribute in discussion
Day 2: attempt as many WAT and SRT items as you can; be yourself
Days 3–4: be active and cooperative in GTO tasks; rest well before your interview
Day 5: stay relaxed and honest in the conference

notes.p:
Mix with your group, help others, eat and sleep well. The board's staff observe candidates informally too, so ordinary courtesy and cheerfulness count. Avoid discussing "tricks" with other candidates the night before tests — it only adds confusion. Keep your phone use low, follow the centre's rules and timings, and treat everyone — staff and fellow candidates — with respect.

A sample daily schedule in the final month: 6:00 run and exercise; 8:00 newspaper; 10:00–12:00 written-exam or OIR practice; 4:00 TAT/WAT/SRT practice; 6:00 GD or lecturette with friends; 9:00 review the day and plan tomorrow.
Small daily habits beat last-minute cramming for the SSB.
points: Start SSB prep alongside the written exam
Fitness daily: running plus strength work
Newspaper daily; form opinions on issues
Timed practice: OIR, PPDT, TAT, WAT, SRT
Weekly GD, lecturette and mock interview
Record yourself speaking and review
At the centre: be helpful, rested and natural
